60:0.2.2.text: You look busy. I'll be here. I'm always here.

60:0.2.3.text: Come back when you've got a night to waste. That's what this takes.

60:0.2.4.text: You've got your hands full. I'm here till October.

60:0.2.5.text: Go do your thing. The plane's not going anywhere. That's the problem.

60:0.2.6.text: Some other time. Old things keep.

60:0.2.7.text: Where'd you come in? Good camp.

side.last.2.text: The sled went to the yard in town.

side.last.3.text: Kari left. She got most of it.

S1.first.text: First stamped: Beat the squad on the Stuart (or Carried the Stuart for Ollie).

S1.leon.text: If you're on it after supper, you'll meet Ollie. Say 'evening' back. That's the whole conversation, the first couple of times.

S1.the-set-piece-the.1.text: Forty-seven. Well. My knees just retired.

S1.the-set-piece-the.2.text: Fifty-three. Not bad. Not forty-nine. Tuesday.

S1.the-set-piece-the.3.text: You carried it twice. That's what I wanted to see. Forty-nine was a younger back than either of ours.

S1.A.1.text: You keep turning up. Either you're slow or you like it here.

S1.A.2.text: Good answer. Most people say it's long.

S1.A.3.text: Me too. Took me twenty minutes to get my boots on tonight.

S1.A.5.text: Tuesdays and Thursdays. Since my wife passed. Doctor said walk. I said where. He said anywhere.

S1.A.6.text: It's the longest one you can drive to. I like to know where the end is.

S1.A.7.text: Carried enough over this one. Rescue squad, thirty-eight years. We trained on the Stuart. Long, wet in the middle, a hill at the end. If you could do it loaded, you could do whatever they called you out for.

S1.A.c7.text: What did they call you out for?

S1.A.8.text: Overdue parties, mostly. Somebody's brother-in-law with a bad ankle. Some years worse.

S1.A.9.text: Squad record, loaded, one trip: forty-nine minutes. Summer of '81. I was on it. Nobody's beat it, mostly because nobody's tried. You want to try, I'll be at the road with my watch. Tuesday or Thursday. Canoe and a pack, one trip, road to river.

S1.A.10.text: Seven o'clock. Don't eat a big supper.

S1.A.11.text: It's not going anywhere. Neither am I, Tuesdays and Thursdays.

S1.A.c11.text: Did you ever meet an old guide on here? Years back.

S1.A.12.text: I meet everybody on here. Guides, Scouts, fellas from Iowa.

S1.A.c12.if: needs: Walt's surname on the Walt page

S1.A.13.text: Walt. Yes. A few times. He'd say evening. I'd say evening.

S1.A.14.text: We didn't have a lot else to say to each other. Some people you've said it all to already.

S1.A.15.text: Do your carry. Then ask me.

S1.A.16.text: Nobody's said that name to me out loud in a long while.

S1.A.17.text: Do your carry. Then ask me again.

S1.A.c14.text: Is it safe to be out here this late?

S1.A.18.text: On a day permit? Then you'd better be in the lot by dark. Rangers don't fine me. I'm too old to be worth the paperwork.

S1.A.19.text: Go on. You'll lose the light. Evening.

S1.B.1.text: Ask me, then. I said I would.
S1.B.1.if: at the river end, needs: the carry done or tried twice

S1.B.c1.text: What was the worst search you were on?

S1.B.2.text: Bald Eagle. October of '77. A young fella, a Finn kid from Ely, went out after ducks and didn't come home. Nine days we dragged.

S1.B.4.text: They said he drowned. I'd carried this portage a hundred times by then. I knew what a canoe does in a wind. His canoe was on the west shore.

S1.B.5.text: It blew nor'west all the day before. Twenty-five, gusts to forty. A loose canoe goes south-east in that. His was upwind. I said so. I'm the only one that did.

S1.B.6.text: Nobody ever asked me where his jacket was, either. Folded. On the rock. Like he'd be right back. Here. It's a copy. I copied everything that fall. Never knew why. It's no good in my truck.

S1.B.w1.text: Ollie Pekkala found Eino, 23 October 1977. The canoe was on the west shore, upwind of a nor'wester. The jacket was folded. Ollie told the sheriff's man. Nobody listened.

S1.B.c4.if: needs: the log page, and Walt's surname known

S1.B.7.text: He was. Walt came to the landing every day of the nine. Sat in his truck. Never came down to the water. When I brought the boy in, Walt had gone home already. I never knew if somebody told him or if he knew.

S1.B.8.text: We said evening on this trail, years later. That was the whole of it. I think it was enough for both of us.

S1.B.c5.text: Walt wrote you knew him before he knew you.
S1.B.c5.if: needs: N12's second ink read, and the line above

S1.B.9.text: Did he. I knew him at the landing in '77. He sat in his truck. He wouldn't have looked at who was on the drag line.

S1.B.c6.text: Walt's canoe was found swamped too.
S1.B.c6.if: needs: the player knows Walt's canoe was on Birch: Sheila's page two, the clipping, or any keeper's "drowned on Birch"

S1.B.11.text: On Birch. I heard. I was off the squad by then.

S1.B.12.text: I went and looked up the weather. Old habit.

S1.B.13.text: And I'm seventy-nine and I walk a portage twice a week so I don't have to think about things like that.

S1.B.14.text: There's a deputy wrote that one up. Novak. I taught her the drag line. She reads weather. Ask her.

S1.B.w2.text: Ollie looked up the wind the night Walt went. He won't say what he thinks.

S1.B.15.text: I dragged lakes. I didn't ask who.

S1.B.16.text: You want who, ask somebody who worked for that outfit. I never did.

S1.C.1.text: Mud's down a foot in the middle.

S1.C.3.text: Bear on the hill Tuesday. Small. Minding its business.

S1.C.4.text: I gave a statement in '77. They wrote down the half they wanted.

S1.C.5.text: Leaves are turning on the hill. Two more weeks of this and I sit.

S1.C.6.text: Last one. Back in June if the knees are.

S1.log.text:
SEARCH — BALD EAGLE L. — HAAPALA, E., 28, Ely

Fri 14 Oct 77. Called 9:40 a.m. Canoe found 7:00 by a Boreal truck crew, W shore
  below the crew landing. Swamped. No paddle. Wool jacket folded on the landing rock.
  Wind NW 15 this a.m. NW 25 g40 yest. per the F.S.
  W SHORE IS UPWIND. Told the sheriff's man. He said canoes do funny things.
Sat 15 – Thu 20. Grid off the landing. Drags, 4 boats. F.S. Beaver Sat, Mon.
  Outfitters' boats Sun. Divers Sun – Wed, vis. 6 ft and going.
Fri 21, Sat 22. Snow squalls. Drags.
Sun 23, 11:15 a.m. Found. My line. Approx. 40 ft, 300 m off the crew landing.
  Bruise L temple.
9 days. Brother at the landing every day.

S2.notice.text:
THE TWIN PORTS TATTLER
pays CASH for photographs of
WHAT WALKS THE RIDGE AT BIG MOOSE LAKE
Night photos welcome. Clear ones preferred.
See Duane, weekends, green pickup in the lot.
"The Truth Is Up North"

S2.leon.1.text: There's a tabloid in Duluth paying for Sasquatch pictures again…

S2.leon.2.text: Duane's harmless. He'll show you the footprint. Let him. It's his whole summer.

S2.conv.1.text: You going in at Big Moose? Then you're my guy. Duane. I write for the Tattler. Don't laugh, it pays for the gas.

S2.conv.2.text: Weekly out of Duluth. Gas stations, bait shops. 'Lake Superior Monster Seen Off Two Harbors.' That one was a log. I said so in the article. They cut that part.

S2.conv.3.text: That's the question. Fella from the Range heard it in '87. Two legs, heavy, on the ridge at the west end. Every few summers somebody hears it again.

S2.conv.c3.text: That's a bear. The back foot's set down on the front one.
S2.conv.c3.if: needs: S4's tracks; the dot on the cast reads "Bear. Hind foot over the front."

S2.conv.5.text: That's what my wife said. She's never been up here.

S2.conv.6.text: Twice. Once in '09, two in the morning. Tall as the tent. Once in '09. Taller than the tent, easy.

S2.conv.7.text: Twenty for a clear picture of anything that was up there at night. We run those too. 'Mystery Solved.' Readers like that, a little. Two hundred for something we can't explain. And the cover.

S2.conv.8.text: The west site, under the ridge. Two stars, lousy landing, alders. Nobody wants it. That's what makes it good.

S2.conv.c7.text: What if it comes down to the tent?

S2.conv.9.text: Me, if it gets bad, I sleep in the canoe. Tied off a ways out. They don't swim. Probably.

S2.conv.10.text: Batteries in your lamp? Good. Don't use it. You'll scare it.

S2.conv.11.text: That's a moose. That's a good moose, though. Twenty.

S2.conv.12.text: A cow in deadfall walks slow, front and back nearly together. I could see it. I'm not saying I see it.

S2.conv.13.text: Oh, look at him. Standing up like a fella at a bar.

S2.conv.14.text: Twenty. 'Two Legs: Solved.' I'll write it myself.

S2.conv.15.text: Moose. Even I know that one.

S2.conv.17.text: Slept through it? Everybody does the first time. The site's not going anywhere.

S2.conv.20.text: Two hundred. And the cover. Your name on it or not, your call.

S2.sold.2.text: You won't regret it. You might. People will say things at the counter.

S2.sold.3.text: Saw your picture in the Tattler. Tall fella.

S2.sold.4.text: Big Moose, huh? I'm not camping there.

S2.sold.5.text: You're famous in four gas stations.

S2.slowyear.text: Fella from Iowa sent in a picture of his brother-in-law in a ghillie suit. We ran it. It's been a slow year.

S3.first.text: First stamped: Logged the northern lights.

S3.notice.text:
LIGHTS OVER FOURTOWN?
Seen something? Write it in the sky book at the counter.
Time, direction, colour, how long. A picture if you have one.
— E.S.

S3.skybook.text:
FOURTOWN — SEPT / OCT — what to look for. (E.S.)

Northern lights: watch the forecast I pin on the board. A strong night, look north after 11.
The train: clear nights, an hour or two after dark. A line of moving dots, low in the west, climbing.
Fog lanterns: a calm night after a warm day. Somebody's lantern on a branch looks like it floats.
Foxfire: a wet week. Rotten birch, at the ground. Green. Doesn't move.
The moon spoils all of it. New moon is best.
Anything else: write it down anyway.

S3.binder.text:
Sept 3. Fourtown N end, 11:10 pm. "Blue lights moving across the sky in a line!!!" — Hendersons, Ames IA
   [Satellites. A train of them, launched this spring. Pass times are on the sheet. E.S.]
Sept 9. Fourtown, the narrows, 1 am. Green curtains N, then red at the top. — a solo, Duluth
   [Northern lights. Strong night. A good one. E.S.]
Sept 14. "Light floating over the water in the fog, moving slow, then gone." — two guys from Chicago
   [A lantern at the north site. They were camped there. I asked. E.S.]
Sept 20. "Green glow in the woods by the shore, low." — Troop 212
   [Foxfire. A fungus in rotten wood. Bring me a piece. E.S.]

S3.lantern.text:
**A fog lantern** | A calm night after a warm day, with a scheduled party at a north-end site | A light that floats and drifts. Paddle toward it: a party's lantern on a branch. They say: "Oh, hey. Are you the lights guy?"
**Foxfire** | A wet week, any night | A faint green glow at ground level on the north shore. Ashore, E on the log: **Foxfire**, a glowing chunk that can be carried. It is dark by morning
**The one light** | Below | Never explained

S3.voices.text:
**Voices carrying** | A late party at a north-end site (a scheduled party when one is there; a scripted one otherwise), 3 km off, talking at their fire. The player hears every word, as clear as across a table: "…no, the *other* bag…" / "Is that somebody's light down there?" | The ear's half of Elaine's lesson: on a calm night the lake carries everything, both ways
**A moose in the narrows** | Splashing in the dark, steady, crossing; against the sky's last glow a long head and a hump, swimming. It climbs out on the far side and shakes like a dog | Not every big shape in the dark is something to fear

S3.match.text: A match carries a mile over water on a calm night. A headlamp, five. That's the one thing I'd teach everybody who goes in.

S3.conv.1.text: You want the sky book. Everybody does, eventually. Sit, it's heavy.

S3.conv.2.text: Everything's something. I taught earth science thirty-one years, and every light a kid ever saw was something.

S3.conv.3.text: Most of them are satellites now. They put up a new train every month.

S3.conv.4.text: Not yet. Once, sort of. I wrote 'boat' on it. I'm not proud of 'boat'.

S3.conv.5.text: It's long and it runs north and south, so you see the whole north sky from the bottom of it. And it's close enough to the road for people from Iowa.

S3.conv.6.text: There's an old story the loggers told, about the cook from the camp going looking for his crew with a lantern. You'll hear it at the bait counter. It's a nice story. It's not science.

S3.conv.7.text: Strong night. That's the sun, a couple of days ago, arriving. Write it in.

S3.conv.8.text: That's them. A string of them, new this spring. They'll spread out and you'll stop noticing. Write it in.

S3.conv.9.text: Was there a site up there? Then there was a lantern. Fog makes a lantern stand on nothing. Write it in.

S3.conv.10.text: Oh, nice. Fungus, in rotten wood. It glows because it can. It'll be out by tomorrow. Write it in.

S3.conv.11.text: You've got a face on. Tell me.

S3.conv.c4.text: Low, steady, over the north bay.

S3.conv.c6.text: It went out when I turned my lamp on.

S3.conv.13.text: There's no boat on Fourtown at one in the morning without a motor.

S3.conv.15.text: Lanterns go downwind, if they go anywhere.

S3.conv.16.text: Somebody with a light who saw yours.

S3.conv.17.text: Then where was their canoe in the morning?

S3.conv.18.text: First one I've written with nothing in front of it.

S3.conv.c7.text: Walt wrote it in his own book too. With a question mark.

S3.conv.20.text: In his own book. Then he wasn't being polite to me. He believed it.

S3.conv.22.text: Two. You're keeping at it. Here. September of 2012.

S3.walt.square.text:
Sept 29. Four Towns, night of the 28th, from the S site, the long rock. N bay,
low, steady, then gone. Kept the red on. The low one stayed till I showed white. W.

S3.conv.23.text: I wrote 'boat' and then I put a question mark on it. I'd forgotten that.

S3.conv.24.text: Walt something. Finnish. He came in on his way out for white gas and saw the book and wrote in it. That's all he wrote.

S3.conv.25.text: He said a fella should keep a red glass for his lamp, so the lake doesn't know where he is. I thought it was the kind of thing old guides say.

S3.conv.26.text: He camped at the south site, the long rock. He drowned, later, I heard.

S3.conv.c9.text: What does 'kept the red on' mean?

S3.conv.27.text: A red lamp. Easy on your eyes at night, and you can see the sky past it. He'd have had his own. They never buy one, the old ones. They make one.

S3.conv.w1.text: Walt wrote in Elaine's sky book in 2012, the day after N09's night. 'Kept the red on.'

S3.conv.28.text: Go on. Dark of the moon's next Tuesday. You know where I'll be. Here.

S3.first2.text: First stamped: Logged the northern lights; Saw the light on Fourtown (the one light).

S4.first.text: First stamped: Wolves answered; Counted the pups.

S4.notice.text:
VOLUNTEER WANTED — WOLF SURVEY
Nina Moose to Agnes. Night work. Some mud.
Must be able to sit still and keep quiet. Pays a little.
Ask for Kari (Fridays) or leave a note with Leon.

S4.the-set-pieces.c2.text: Wolves. One big, some small. This morning.

S4.the-set-pieces.c3.text: Moose, a cow and a calf.

S4.the-set-pieces.c5.text: Two men, boots. Came by water and left the same way.

S4.the-set-pieces.c6.text: One man, boots. Sat a long while.

S4.wall.text: If it sounds like it came off a wall, it did.

S4.conv.1.text: Are you the one asking about the notice? Hi. Kari. I count wolves. Well. I listen to wolves and then I do math.

S4.conv.2.text: I need the pack's range before my grant runs out. They howl, I howl, I write down where the answer came from. Three places, three lines, they cross where the wolves are.

S4.conv.3.text: You'd be a second pair of ears. I've only got the two.

S4.conv.4.text: Badly. It works anyway. They're not critics. Let them.

S4.conv.5.text: They want nothing to do with you. Hang your food. Don't leave fish guts on the rock. That's the whole danger.

S4.conv.c4.text: Why do you care where they are?

S4.conv.6.text: Because people are going to argue about them either way, and I'd like them to argue about real numbers.

S4.conv.7.text: Half the county thinks there's too many and the other half thinks there's too few. I think there's one pack on Agnes and I'd like to know how many pups.

S4.conv.8.text: Nothing. Not where. Not the den, not the pups. Please.

S4.conv.c7.text: An old guide heard wolves on Agnes, and the loons answered.

S4.conv.10.text: That could be this pack's grandparents.

S4.conv.11.text: Loons do that, sometimes. Nobody knows why. I'd love to know why.

S4.conv.12.text: Bring a sweater. Three in the morning is a different month.

S4.conv.13.text: Here. Front foot. See how the toes sit tight, like it's going somewhere? A dog's go everywhere. And the front's bigger than the back. Front feet carry the weight.

S4.conv.14.text: That's it. That's the whole class.

S4.conv.15.text: Where'd your lines cross? That's good. That's west of the lake, in the primitive area. I can't send you in there. The Forest Service can, for a fee.

S4.conv.16.text: In August the pups'll be out of the den and in a meadow. If you can count them from a long way off, that's my whole summer.

S4.conv.17.text: Five? Five pups. Okay. That's a good year.

S4.conv.18.text: You're the one helping the wolf girl. Lyle. I shoot calendars. Pups at a rendezvous in August light, that's a cover. I'd pay sixty bucks for a ring on my map. I'd stay back. Way back. I've got the lens for it.

S4.conv.19.text: Fair enough. Can't blame a guy.

S4.conv.21.text: Are you the wolf person? Can I see one? I won't touch it.

S4.conv.22.text: We'd just like to hear them. From the site's fine.

S4.conv.c10.text: Listen tonight, from here. They'll howl.

S4.conv.23.text: THEY HOWLED. I was awake. I was so awake.

S4.conv.c11.text: There's a meadow west of the lake.

S4.kept.2.text: Kari says you kept your mouth shut. That's rarer than wolves.

S4.moved.1.text: They moved. People came. It happens.

S4.moved.2.text: Heard somebody put a photographer on the pups. Not you, I hope.

S4.kari.text:
Agnes pack, summer 2026. Adults: 4–5. Pups: 5 (counted 14 Aug).
Range: roughly 120 km², centred west of Agnes. Den and rendezvous: not given.
Thanks to a volunteer canoeist for three nights of bad howling and good bearings.
— K.V.

S4.abandoned.text: Rendezvous abandoned 18 Aug (disturbance). Pups: not counted.

S4.left.text: Kari left. Said she got most of it.

S5.the-pilots-chart-book.c1.text: straight cut — good to steer by

S5.the-pilots-chart-book.w1.text: The pilot's straight cut ends here. The notch.

S5.conv.1.text: You headed toward the Kek? Then I've got a question. You ever see an airplane in a lake?

S5.conv.2.text: My grandpa's. Red and cream, on skis. He put it through the ice on the Kek in December of 1950, hauling Christmas for a lodge. Swam out the hole. Walked to the lodge in wet wool.

S5.conv.3.text: He told it every Christmas till he died. Always said he left his good map case in it.

S5.conv.4.text: South shore. Near the portage. That's what he said.

S5.conv.5.text: The case. Grandpa's charts were in it. My mom has every other thing he owned and none of his maps.

S5.conv.6.text: And it'd be something to find. I find sunglasses all summer.

S5.conv.c4.text: What if I find it first?

S5.conv.7.text: Then you found it first. I'd want to see the chart, that's all. Grandpa drew all over his charts.

S5.conv.c5.text: An old guide saw red and cream off the north shore.
S5.conv.c5.if: needs: N11 read; or the keeper's rumour

S5.conv.8.text: North? …North. Grandpa said near the portage. Grandpa said a lot of things.

S5.conv.9.text: If I find it, I owe you. I'll put the chart up here where everybody can see it.

S5.conv.10.text: Calm days only. Anything over five and you can't see your own feet.

S5.conv.13.text: I'm putting this on the wall here. Anybody can come look. That's what he'd want. He loved an audience.

S5.conv.w1.text: The pilot's chart, on the Round Lake wall

S5.conv.15.text: Can I take a picture of the chart, at least? Mom'll want to see his hand.

S5.conv.c10.text: Is there a plane in the Kek?

S5.conv.18.text: There is. December of '50, the winter before they shut the sky. Everybody was flying everything while they still could. Fella on skis came down on new ice off the Kek and it took him.

S5.conv.19.text: Swam out. Walked to the lodge. Ten below. Lived to be old, I heard. The lodge didn't. Lost its whole Christmas, and the next year there were no more planes.

S5.conv.21.text: Red and cream. That's right. I've had it yellow for fifty years.

S5.conv.22.text: Never saw it. The Round Lake people have a fella diving for it.

S5.conv.c14.if: needs: N11 read, Hap's trust from the guiding arc

S5.conv.23.text: Walt asked me about that plane. Wanted to know if anybody died in it. I said no. He said good, then he'd said a word over it for nothing.

S6.how-it-starts.1.text: Pekka's dad ran whiskey when he was sixteen…

S6.ledger.text:
1928
May 30   over the slide           14 cs     pd. men  $9.00
June 2   up river, 3 carries      14 cs
June 3   in the pit               12 cs     2 broke
June 3   Niemi kid — carrying               .50
June 3   Ahola kid — carrying               .50
June 10  Mr. K.                             $20.00
June 10  the constable            2 cs
Sept 28  last in the pit          11 cs
Jan 12 '29  road not froze. truck stuck at camp.
Mar 2 '29   got 10 cs out by sled. 1 cs broke, left it.

S6.conv.1.text: You've got the look. Old maps? Bottles? Anything with a date on it? Orrin. I collect. Not junk. History.

S6.conv.2.text: Prohibition, mostly. Ledgers, labels, a bottle with the seal on. Up here it's all rumours and broken glass.

S6.conv.c2.if: needs: the story from Aili or René, or N08

S6.conv.3.text: Oh, you've heard it. Down from the Canadian side, over Lac La Croix. Over the Beatty, where the rails are now. Up the Sioux against the water, every carry on it, past where the road goes over. Then a little lake off the east side with a beaver pond at the back.

S6.conv.4.text: You know what they call that lake now?

S6.conv.5.text: That's how you know it's true. I've looked there. Twice. I looked on the wrong side of the pond.

S6.conv.6.text: Bootleg. That's how you know it's true.

S6.conv.7.text: Ten summers. My knees, the bugs, and I'm a better buyer than a finder.

S6.conv.c6.text: Do you buy old papers? Mining things?

S6.conv.8.text: Mining? Lord, no. Nobody collects mining. It's all numbers.

S6.conv.9.text: Depends what it is. Bring it and we'll see.
S6.conv.9.if: before the pit; with the ledger

S6.conv.10.text: For a runner's book? Two-fifty. Cash. Today.

S6.conv.c8.text: What will you do with it?

S6.conv.11.text: Keep it. Look at it. Maybe pass it on to somebody who'll appreciate it.

S6.conv.14.text: Niemi kid. Carrying. Fifty cents. Pekka always said his dad was the boss of the river.

S6.conv.15.text: Fifty cents. Pekka would've loved that.

S6.conv.16.text: He said he carved his name at the Beatty. I thought that was a joke too.

S6.conv.17.text: That rye came from our side. Legal over here, mostly. My grandfather sold to them. Different country, different law. Same lake.

S6.conv.18.text: I'll open it at a funeral. Probably mine. You're invited.

S7.the-place.w2.text: Mummo's. The rock where the brothers learned to swim. The young one was better.

S7.notice.text:
PHOTO WANTED: LILACS in bloom at the old places on Basswood,
for the church calendar. June only. $25 for a good one.
— Rose G. (Tuesdays, the café table by the window)

S7.the-set-piece.c1.text: the lilacs at the old camp

S7.the-set-piece.1.text: There's a bed in the woods. A metal one. Is somebody buried there?

S7.the-set-piece.4.text: You can jump off here. It's deep. My dad says it's not deep. It's deep.

S7.conv.1.text: You're the one with the notice? Sit. I can't get out there any more and I'd like to see them.

S7.conv.2.text: Ours, for one. Gornik's, on the big part of the lake. Bought out in '64. My dad and my uncles burned it on the ice the next February. Better than watching.

S7.conv.3.text: Took me thirty years to be glad they did it. My dad never got there.

S7.conv.4.text: Everywhere there was a woman with a cutting. Ours are gone, the beavers had them. Try past Prairie. There was a Finn fish camp there. An old lady and two boys who swam like otters. The boys called her Mummo. Everybody did.

S7.conv.5.text: Haapala. The young one drowned, later.

S7.conv.6.text: Guided. Walt. He's gone too now. That family's had it hard.

S7.conv.8.text: That's the step. I sat on that step with a bottle of pop in 1956.

S7.conv.9.text: I'll put it in for June.

S7.conv.10.text: Go on. Don't let me keep you. I'll keep myself.

S7.end.text: Lilacs every June. Rose has the picture.

S8.tom.text: You going to Insula? Look at the sled on the lunch rock before my crew gets to it. Tell me if it's history. I honestly can't.

S8.rumour.1.text: Tom Becker's crew is going to haul that old sled off the lunch rock on Insula. People have opinions.

S8.rumour.2.text: There's a sled on a rock on Insula. Half the town wants it gone and the other half eats lunch next to it.

S8.the-set-piece-a.c1.text: Cut stump, knee high. Cut long ago, standing in snow.

S8.the-set-piece-a.c2.text: A square hollow. Something stood here.

S8.the-set-piece-a.c4.text: Rusted things in a row along one side.

S8.conv.1.text: Where'd you come in? Good camp.

S8.conv.2.text: It's on my list. 'Remove: sled, two window sashes, Insula lunch rock.' Somebody wrote it after the fire. I've been not doing it for three summers.

S8.conv.3.text: Over fifty years old, it's heritage and I'm not allowed to touch it. Under fifty, it's junk and I'm supposed to haul it. Nobody knows which. I'm supposed to know which.

S8.conv.4.text: My crew's on Insula the third week of September. If nobody's told me anything by then, it goes.

S8.conv.c4.text: What would an old cabin site look like?

S8.conv.5.text: Stumps at knee height, cut flat, from a man standing in snow. A square hollow where the floor was. Rusted things in a row along one wall. Everything else grows over.

S8.conv.6.text: That's what they taught me. I've found two.

S8.conv.c5.text: Where would the cabin have been?
S8.conv.c5.if: needs: Tom met twice, or asked a week after the first meeting

S8.conv.7.text: I looked in the old files after you asked. 'Trapper's cabin, burned 1956, creek on the far shore from the narrows.' That's all it says. Nobody wrote down which creek.

S8.conv.8.text: Everything looks old to me. I need something I can write down.

S8.conv.c7.text: I found where it came from.

S8.conv.10.text: That's a cabin. That's an old one.

S8.conv.11.text: Well, that's got a date on it.

S8.conv.12.text: Sixty years on the rock, then. At least.

S8.conv.13.text: Emil. I'll write 'Emil' down. That'll be the first time anybody has.

S8.conv.15.text: That's good enough for me. I'll write it up as heritage. It stays where it is and nobody gets to move it. Including me.

S8.conv.16.text: My boss'll want the tin. Can I take it?

S8.conv.c12.text: Was there a trapper on Insula?

S8.conv.19.text: Emil. My dad knew him. Wintered on Insula from the thirties till they made him quit. Came out in March with his furs on a sled and stopped at every resort on the way for coffee. Took him a week to go twenty miles.

S8.conv.20.text: Up a creek on the far side from where you eat lunch. Dad said Emil went straight across the ice from that rock to his creek. Straight. Never went around anything in his life.

S8.conv.c14.text: Why's the sled on the rock?

S8.conv.21.text: The way I heard it, they burned his cabin after he quit, and the next March he went back for his windows, because glass cost money. Ice went bad at the narrows. He left the sled on the rock to come back for. Never did.

S8.conv.22.text: Everybody's been leaving it there for him since.

S8.conv.23.text: We've eaten lunch on that rock since 1968. The sled was there the first time. So were the windows. Glass in both.

S8.conv.24.text: Two panes. Vern broke one in '74.

S8.conv.26.text: Got one of Vern in '68 with a pike on the sled. He looks about twelve.

S8.conv.w1.text: Vern Ostby with a pike, the lunch rock, Lake Insula, August 1968

S8.conv.27.text: The one with the beaver house at the mouth, straight across. Dad pointed it out the first year.

S8.conv.30.text: It's a wilderness. Take the junk out. That's the whole point of it.

S8.conv.31.text: You take that sled out and you take out the only thing on Insula with a story on it.

S8.end.text: It's in the yard in town. If you ever find out how old it was, tell me. I'll feel bad on schedule.

S9.rumour.text: There's an old coffee pot off the Alice beach site. Every kid who camps there's lost a lure on it. Half the jigs in Alice are in that pot.

S9.kid.1.text: There's a pot down there. Dad says it's a rock. It's a pot.

S9.how-it-starts.1.text: The blue one. He lost it off a rock somewhere.

S9.pot.dot.text: Blue enamel coffee pot. A chip on the lip.

S9.kid.2.text: You got a big one! Is it a big one?

S9.kid.3.1.text: YOU GOT IT. Can I hold it?

S9.kid.3.2.text: It's heavy. It's got sand in it. Dad, it's a pot.

S9.kid.3.4.text: You can keep it. I just wanted to know.

S9.conv.1.text: You got the Alice pot. Forty years of kids and their jigs. Huh.

S9.conv.2.text: Don't lose it off a rock.

S9.pot.identity.text: Blue enamel, a chip on the lip

S9.first.text: First stamped: Brought up June's pot.

S10.0.1.text: The paintings on North Hegman are older than anybody can say. Look from the canoe. Don't touch them.

60:11.1.text: Evening. Saw the paper. They printed the wind.

60:11.3.text: They put Walt's picture up at the store. I saw it Tuesday.

60:11.4.text: I don't do the calendar any more.
